claim: Falciparum malaria is clinically heterogeneous.
source: Falciparum malaria is clinically heterogeneous and the relative contribution of parasite and host in shaping disease severity remains unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract about the clinical presentation of falciparum malaria.

claim: The relative contribution of parasite and host in shaping disease severity remains unclear.
source: Falciparum malaria is clinically heterogeneous and the relative contribution of parasite and host in shaping disease severity remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Some volunteers remained quiescent in response to blood challenge.
source: We uncovered marked heterogeneity in the host response to blood challenge; some volunteers remained quiescent, others triggered interferon-stimulated inflammation and some showed transcriptional evidence of myeloid cell suppression.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptional profiling data showing no measurable response in some volunteers.

claim: Some volunteers triggered interferon-stimulated inflammation in response to blood challenge.
source: We uncovered marked heterogeneity in the host response to blood challenge; some volunteers remained quiescent, others triggered interferon-stimulated inflammation and some showed transcriptional evidence of myeloid cell suppression.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptional profiling and plasma chemokine measurements.

claim: Some volunteers showed transcriptional evidence of myeloid cell suppression.
source: We uncovered marked heterogeneity in the host response to blood challenge; some volunteers remained quiescent, others triggered interferon-stimulated inflammation and some showed transcriptional evidence of myeloid cell suppression.
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis showing downregulation of myeloid-associated genes.

claim: Only inflammatory volunteers experienced hallmark symptoms of malaria.
source: Significantly, only inflammatory volunteers experienced hallmark symptoms of malaria.
evidence: This is supported by clinical scoring data and correlation with inflammatory markers.

claim: There was no transcriptional evidence for preferential expansion of group A or DC8 var genes in naive hosts.
source: When we tracked temporal changes in parasite VSA expression to ask whether variants associated with severe disease rapidly expand in naive hosts, we found no transcriptional evidence to support this hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data comparing var gene expression at the start and end of infection.

claim: Parasite variants that dominate severe malaria do not have an intrinsic growth or survival advantage.
source: These data indicate that parasite variants that dominate severe malaria do not have an intrinsic growth or survival advantage; instead, they presumably rely upon infection-induced changes in their within-host environment for selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of preferential expansion of group A/DC8 variants during the study period.

claim: Parasite variants associated with severe disease rely upon infection-induced changes in their within-host environment for selection.
source: These data indicate that parasite variants that dominate severe malaria do not have an intrinsic growth or survival advantage; instead, they presumably rely upon infection-induced changes in their within-host environment for selection.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the absence of intrinsic growth advantage.

claim: There is enormous diversity in the human response to identical immune challenge.
source: There is enormous diversity in the human response to identical immune challenge.
evidence: This is supported by references to large cohort studies examining immune variation.

claim: Heterogeneity in the host response to Plasmodium falciparum is well-recognised.
source: Controlled human malaria infection (CHMI) provides a well-established challenge model in which to examine immune variation in vivo, and heterogeneity in the host response to Plasmodium falciparum is well-recognised (Roestenberg et al., 2012; Yap et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous CHMI studies.

claim: Prior work suggests a dichotomy in immune decision-making with some individuals triggering an inflammatory response characterized by high circulating levels of IFNγ.
source: Prior work suggests a dichotomy in immune decision-making with some individuals triggering an inflammatory response, which is characterised by high circulating levels of IFNγ, whilst others mount an alternative response distinguished by the early release of TGFβ and suppression of IFNγ signalling (de Jong et al., 2020; Harpaz et al., 1992; Walther et al., 2005; Walther et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some individuals mount an alternative response distinguished by the early release of TGFβ and suppression of IFNγ signalling.
source: Prior work suggests a dichotomy in immune decision-making with some individuals triggering an inflammatory response, which is characterised by high circulating levels of IFNγ, whilst others mount an alternative response distinguished by the early release of TGFβ and suppression of IFNγ signalling (de Jong et al., 2020; Harpaz et al., 1992; Walther et al., 2005; Walther et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The precise mechanisms underpinning divergent immune responses remain unknown.
source: The precise mechanisms underpinning these divergent responses remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Previous CHMI studies have revealed an upregulation of genes associated with pathogen detection, NFκB activation, and IFNγ signalling consistent with a systemic inflammatory response.
source: Genome-wide transcriptional profiling has the potential to map immune decision-making in unprecedented detail and previous CHMI studies have revealed an upregulation of genes associated with pathogen detection, NFκB activation, and IFNγ signalling consistent with a systemic inflammatory response (Ockenhouse et al., 2006; Tran et al., 2019; Tran et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous transcriptional profiling studies.

claim: A transcriptional signature of an alternative immune response has not been described in naive hosts.
source: A transcriptional signature of an alternative immune response has not been described in naive hosts.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior findings.

claim: Prior studies were primarily designed to measure shared or common signatures of infection, potentially masking variation between volunteers.
source: Nevertheless, these prior studies were primarily designed to measure shared or common signatures of infection, potentially masking variation between volunteers.
evidence: This is an inference about the design limitations of previous studies.

claim: One study has specifically investigated transcriptional variation in CHMI and reported two distinct outcomes based on host microRNA profiles.
source: Only one study (Burel et al., 2017) has specifically investigated transcriptional variation in CHMI and it reported two distinct outcomes based on host microRNA profiles; notably, the authors were able to correlate the induction of three specific miRNAs with a lower parasite burden suggesting that events early in infection may have important downstream consequences.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The induction of three specific miRNAs correlates with a lower parasite burden.
source: Only one study (Burel et al., 2017) has specifically investigated transcriptional variation in CHMI and it reported two distinct outcomes based on host microRNA profiles; notably, the authors were able to correlate the induction of three specific miRNAs with a lower parasite burden suggesting that events early in infection may have important downstream consequences.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Events early in infection may have important downstream consequences.
source: Only one study (Burel et al., 2017) has specifically investigated transcriptional variation in CHMI and it reported two distinct outcomes based on host microRNA profiles; notably, the authors were able to correlate the induction of three specific miRNAs with a lower parasite burden suggesting that events early in infection may have important downstream consequences.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on findings from a cited study.

claim: Direct intravenous challenge with blood-stage parasites ensures all volunteers receive an identical immune challenge.
source: In this context, direct intravenous challenge with blood-stage parasites provides a unique opportunity to assess the contribution of host-intrinsic mechanisms of variation as it ensures all volunteers receive an identical immune challenge (Duncan and Draper, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation and is a characteristic of the blood challenge model.

claim: Expression of group A and DC8 var genes is associated with severe malaria in both children and adults.
source: Expression of a subset of parasite variant surface antigens (VSA) known as group A and DC8 var genes is associated with severe malaria in both children and adults (Duffy et al., 2019; Jespersen et al., 2016; Kyriacou et al., 2006; Lavstsen et al., 2012; Tonkin-Hill et al., 2018; Warimwe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Group A and DC8 var genes encode PfEMP1 adhesion molecules that mediate sequestration of infected red cells in the microvasculature.
source: These virulence-associated genes encode PfEMP1 adhesion molecules that mediate sequestration of infected red cells in the microvasculature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of these genes.

claim: Group A/DC8-expressing parasites are thought to be more pathogenic than those expressing other var types (groups B and C).
source: Group A/DC8-expressing parasites are thought to be more pathogenic than those expressing other var types (groups B and C) and can bind the endothelium with high affinity in sensitive sites, such as brain (Jensen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents current understanding in the field.

claim: Group A/DC8-expressing parasites can bind the endothelium with high affinity in sensitive sites, such as brain.
source: Group A/DC8-expressing parasites are thought to be more pathogenic than those expressing other var types (groups B and C) and can bind the endothelium with high affinity in sensitive sites, such as brain (Jensen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: It is unknown whether expression of group A/DC8 variants can influence the immune response.
source: It is unknown whether expression of these variants can influence the immune response, for example by causing dysregulated activation that leads to widespread collateral tissue damage.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: It is unknown whether inflammation might preferentially support the survival and expansion of group A/DC8 variants by upregulating their binding sites on the endothelium.
source: Or conversely, whether inflammation might preferentially support the survival and expansion of these variants by upregulating their binding sites on the endothelium.
evidence: This is a statement about an unanswered question in the field.

claim: Parasites transcribe a broad array of var genes in naive hosts, with predominant expression of group B variants and no marked differences between volunteers.
source: It has been observed in previous CHMI studies that parasites transcribe a broad array of var genes in naive hosts, with predominant expression of group B variants and no marked differences between volunteers (Bachmann et al., 2019; Bachmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous CHMI studies.

claim: Mosquitoes reset malaria parasites to ensure diverse expression of their VSA repertoire at the start of the blood cycle.
source: Indeed, we have shown that mosquitoes reset malaria parasites to ensure diverse expression of their VSA repertoire at the start of the blood cycle (Spence et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: It remains unclear how group A and DC8 var genes come to dominate the PfEMP1 landscape in severe malaria.
source: It therefore remains unclear how group A and DC8 var genes come to dominate the PfEMP1 landscape in severe malaria.
evidence: This is a statement about an unresolved question in the field.

claim: Antibody-mediated clearance of parasites expressing group B variants is unlikely to explain dominance of group A/DC8 variants because severe malaria develops in hosts with low or absent immunity during their first few infections of life.
source: Antibody-mediated clearance of parasites expressing group B variants is a possible explanation, but is unlikely because severe malaria develops in hosts with low or absent immunity during their first few infections of life (Gonçalves et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claim: It has been suggested that parasites expressing group A/DC8 var genes rapidly and preferentially expand because they have an intrinsic growth and/or survival advantage in naive hosts.
source: It has instead been suggested that parasites expressing group A/DC8 var genes rapidly and preferentially expand because they have an intrinsic growth and/or survival advantage in naive hosts (Abdi et al., 2017; Bull et al., 2000; Jensen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous hypotheses in the literature.

claim: The hypothesis that group A/DC8 variants have an intrinsic growth advantage is widely accepted but is not based on substantial evidence.
source: This explanation is widely accepted but is not based on substantial evidence.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the current state of evidence.

claim: A cohort of 14 malaria-naive volunteers were infected with an equal number of blood-stage parasites (clone 3D7) by direct intravenous inoculation.
source: To explore host-intrinsic variation in the immune response to P. falciparum, a cohort of 14 malaria-naive volunteers were infected with an equal number of blood-stage parasites (clone 3D7) by direct intravenous inoculation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: The pathogenic blood cycle was initiated in every volunteer within a 30-min window.
source: This enabled the pathogenic blood cycle to be initiated in every volunteer within a 30-min window (Payne et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation and describes a feature of the blood challenge model.

claim: Systemic changes in the host response were captured through time by transcriptionally profiling whole blood every 48 hr from the day before infection until the day of diagnosis.
source: Systemic changes in the host response were then captured through time by transcriptionally profiling whole blood every 48 hr from the day before infection until the day of diagnosis (the point of drug treatment).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The time-point of diagnosis varied between volunteers, occurring 7.5–10.5 days post-infection.
source: This time-point varied between volunteers, occurring 7.5–10.5 days post-infection when two out of three diagnostic criteria were met (positive thick blood smear and/or parasite density >500 parasites ml−1 by qPCR and/or symptoms consistent with malaria).
evidence: This describes the variability in time to diagnosis in the study.

claim: Variance in one third of infected volunteers (4/14) was comparable to the uninfected control group.
source: We found that variance in one third of infected volunteers (4/14) was comparable to the uninfected control group, suggesting these four volunteers did not respond to infection (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression variance.

claim: Four volunteers (v018, v012, v208, and v020) failed to cross both thresholds for a measurable response and were therefore grouped and labelled unresponsive.
source: Using the variance and distance travelled metrics, we then set two thresholds to identify volunteers that triggered a measurable response to blood challenge (see Materials and methods); four volunteers failed to cross both thresholds (v018, v012, v208, and v020) and were therefore grouped and labelled unresponsive.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of transcriptional data.

claim: There were zero differentially expressed genes in the unresponsive group at diagnosis compared to pre-infection.
source: A pairwise comparison between the diagnosis and pre-infection samples obtained from these four volunteers confirmed that there were zero differentially expressed genes in this group (adj p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Immune quiescence is a common outcome of controlled human malaria infection.
source: Immune quiescence is therefore a common outcome of controlled human malaria infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that 4/14 volunteers showed no response.

claim: The remaining 10 volunteers made a robust response to infection based on variance and distance travelled metrics.
source: In contrast, variance (Figure 1—source data 1) and distance travelled (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) both suggested that the remaining 10 volunteers made a robust response to infection (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of transcriptional data.

claim: Eight volunteers upregulated gene clusters 2 and 4 at diagnosis.
source: Based on this observation, we grouped the eight volunteers who upregulated gene clusters 2 and 4 and performed a pairwise comparison between their diagnosis and pre-infection samples; we uncovered 2028 differentially expressed genes (adj p<0.05) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis and differential gene expression analysis.

claim: 2028 genes were differentially expressed at diagnosis in the inflammatory group compared to pre-infection.
source: Based on this observation, we grouped the eight volunteers who upregulated gene clusters 2 and 4 and performed a pairwise comparison between their diagnosis and pre-infection samples; we uncovered 2028 differentially expressed genes (adj p<0.05) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: ClueGO uncovered 217 GO terms across 34 functional groups for the inflammatory response.
source: ClueGO uncovered 217 GO terms across 34 functional groups (Supplementary file 4); the most significant groups related to interferon signalling, activation of myeloid cells, production of inflammatory molecules, and activation of T cells (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis using ClueGO.

claim: The most significant functional groups in the inflammatory response related to interferon signalling, activation of myeloid cells, production of inflammatory molecules, and activation of T cells.
source: ClueGO uncovered 217 GO terms across 34 functional groups (Supplementary file 4); the most significant groups related to interferon signalling, activation of myeloid cells, production of inflammatory molecules, and activation of T cells (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis.

claim: There was a > 2-fold increase in CXCL9 and/or CXCL10 at diagnosis in every volunteer in the inflammatory group but no other volunteer.
source: We then biologically validated ClueGO's in silico finding by measuring the plasma concentrations of two interferon-stimulated chemokines, CXCL9 and CXCL10. These chemokines are primarily produced by myeloid cells and specifically function to recruit and activate T cells (Groom and Luster, 2011). We found a > 2-fold increase in one or both of these chemokines at diagnosis in every volunteer in this group but no other volunteer (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by plasma protein measurements.

claim: CXCL9 and CXCL10 are primarily produced by myeloid cells and specifically function to recruit and activate T cells.
source: These chemokines are primarily produced by myeloid cells and specifically function to recruit and activate T cells (Groom and Luster, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge about these chemokines.

claim: Two volunteers were grouped as suppressors based on their apparent downregulation of clusters 1 and 3 at diagnosis.
source: The final two volunteers were also grouped (and given the suppressor tag) based on their apparent downregulation of clusters 1 and 3 at diagnosis (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of gene expression data.

claim: 77 genes were differentially expressed in the suppressor group at diagnosis compared to pre-infection.
source: Significantly, a pairwise comparison between their diagnosis and pre-infection samples revealed a core signature of 77 genes that were differentially expressed in response to blood challenge (adj p<0.05, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: The majority of differentially expressed genes in the suppressor group (62/77) were downregulated.
source: The majority of these genes (62/77) were downregulated and crucially >85% were unique to this group, including key regulators of monocyte and neutrophil differentiation (Csf3r) and recruitment and activation (Cxcl7, Cxcr2, Clec4e, Clec7a, and Mnda, Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: >85% of differentially expressed genes in the suppressor group were unique to this group.
source: The majority of these genes (62/77) were downregulated and crucially >85% were unique to this group, including key regulators of monocyte and neutrophil differentiation (Csf3r) and recruitment and activation (Cxcl7, Cxcr2, Clec4e, Clec7a, and Mnda, Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of differentially expressed genes between groups.

claim: 893 genes were differentially expressed between the inflammatory and suppressor groups at diagnosis.
source: A direct pairwise comparison between the inflammatory and suppressor groups confirmed that each of these six immune genes was differentially expressed at diagnosis, together with a further 887 genes (adj p<0.05, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis (6 + 887 = 893).

claim: The host response profiles of inflammatory and suppressor groups do not overlap and likely represent distinct in vivo outcomes of immune decision-making.
source: Evidently, these host response profiles do not overlap and instead likely represent distinct in vivo outcomes of immune decision-making.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential gene expression analysis showing distinct signatures.

claim: There are at least three possible outcomes of blood-stage infection: immune quiescence, interferon-stimulated inflammation, and suppression of myeloid-associated gene expression.
source: Collectively, these data reveal marked variation in the human immune response to falciparum malaria with at least three possible outcomes of blood-stage infection – immune quiescence, interferon-stimulated inflammation, and suppression of myeloid-associated gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Five additional malaria-naive volunteers were inoculated with the same parasite genotype by mosquito bite.
source: We therefore inoculated five additional malaria-naive volunteers with the same parasite genotype but this time by the natural route of infection, mosquito bite (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the mosquito challenge study.

claim: 116 out of 117 genes in the 117-gene superset were upregulated exclusively during the blood cycle after mosquito challenge.
source: When we clustered and visualised the expression data within this superset we found that 116 out of 117 genes were upregulated exclusively during the blood cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression data from mosquito challenge.

claim: Response to interferon gamma (GO: 0034341) was the most significantly enriched GO term in the 117-gene superset from mosquito challenge.
source: And when we examined the biological functions of these genes ClueGO identified response to interferon gamma (GO: 0034341) as the most significantly enriched GO term (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis.

claim: Response to interferon gamma was also the most significant GO term in inflammatory volunteers infected by blood challenge.
source: Notably, this was also the most significant GO term in inflammatory volunteers infected by blood challenge (Supplementary file 4), indicating concordance between the two infection models.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of gene ontology analyses between the two studies.

claim: 19 of the 21 genes that displayed the highest fold change in inflammatory volunteers (blood challenge) were also upregulated in the 117-gene superset (mosquito challenge).
source: In agreement, 19 of the 21 genes that displayed the highest fold change in inflammatory volunteers (blood challenge) were also upregulated in the 117-gene superset (mosquito challenge, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of gene expression data between the two studies.

claim: High circulating levels of CXCL10 were detectable at diagnosis in four of the five volunteers infected by mosquito bite.
source: And at protein level, high circulating levels of CXCL10 were detectable at diagnosis in four of the five volunteers infected by mosquito bite (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by plasma protein measurements.

claim: Interferon-stimulated inflammation is the dominant human response to blood-stage parasites regardless of the route of infection.
source: Our data therefore demonstrate that interferon-stimulated inflammation is the dominant human response to blood-stage parasites regardless of the route of infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the concordance between blood and mosquito challenge studies.

claim: The data fail to provide compelling evidence of a systemic transcriptional response to liver-stage infection in human malaria.
source: Furthermore, our data fail to provide compelling evidence of a systemic transcriptional response to liver-stage infection in human malaria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on the observation that gene expression changes occurred only during the blood cycle.

claim: The pre-erythrocytic-stages of infection may have a limited role in shaping the immune response during the pathogenic blood cycle.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that the pre-erythrocytic-stages of infection may have a limited role in shaping the immune response during the pathogenic blood cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of transcriptional response during liver-stage infection.

claim: The parasite multiplication rate varied considerably between volunteers (range 6.7–12.8).
source: The parasite multiplication rate (PMR, modelled from the qPCR data [Payne et al., 2016]) varied considerably between volunteers (range 6.7–12.8) despite every individual receiving an equal number of infected red cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data and modeling.

claim: The parasite multiplication rate of the inflammatory group was not significantly different to that of unresponsive or suppressor hosts.
source: However, the parasite multiplication rate of the inflammatory group was not significantly different to that of unresponsive or suppressor hosts (Figure 3a–b) and therefore appears to have little bearing on the outcome of immune decision-making.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of parasite multiplication rates between groups.

claim: Inflammatory volunteers tended to have a longer course of infection.
source: Inflammatory volunteers did, however, tend to have a longer course of infection (Figure 3a) and hence the parasite burden at diagnosis was higher for the inflammatory group (median 30,309 parasites ml−1, range 9133–273,247) than the rest of the cohort (median 7899 parasites ml−1, range 1440–19,670) (Mann Whitney test, p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of time to diagnosis and parasite density data.

claim: The parasite burden at diagnosis was higher for the inflammatory group (median 30,309 parasites ml−1) than the rest of the cohort (median 7899 parasites ml−1).
source: Inflammatory volunteers did, however, tend to have a longer course of infection (Figure 3a) and hence the parasite burden at diagnosis was higher for the inflammatory group (median 30,309 parasites ml−1, range 9133–273,247) than the rest of the cohort (median 7899 parasites ml−1, range 1440–19,670) (Mann Whitney test, p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of parasite densities.

claim: Parasite burden may promote an inflammatory response in the blood challenge model but cannot fully explain it.
source: Parasite burden may therefore promote an inflammatory response in this challenge model but cannot fully explain it; for example, 2/4 unresponsive volunteers (v018 and v020) had parasite densities that were comparable to 4/8 inflammatory volunteers at diagnosis (v017, v027, v026, and v106, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some unresponsive volunteers had similar parasite densities to inflammatory volunteers.

claim: The parasite density threshold required to trigger inflammation is highly variable between individuals.
source: Our data therefore support previous observations that the parasite density threshold required to trigger inflammation is highly variable between individuals (Gatton and Cheng, 2002; Molineaux et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Volunteers in the unresponsive and suppressor groups were essentially asymptomatic at diagnosis.
source: Volunteers in the unresponsive and suppressor groups were essentially asymptomatic at diagnosis, whereas inflammatory volunteers exhibited more frequent and/or severe adverse events, including fever (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by clinical symptom data.

claim: Inflammatory volunteers exhibited more frequent and/or severe adverse events, including fever.
source: Volunteers in the unresponsive and suppressor groups were essentially asymptomatic at diagnosis, whereas inflammatory volunteers exhibited more frequent and/or severe adverse events, including fever (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by clinical symptom data.

claim: There was a strong positive correlation between symptoms and the intensity of inflammation.
source: When we then calculated a cumulative clinical score for each volunteer (by summing all adverse events throughout infection) we found a strong positive correlation between symptoms and the intensity of inflammation (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: There was no correlation between clinical score and parasite multiplication rate.
source: In contrast, there was no correlation between clinical score and parasite multiplication rate (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: Only one volunteer displayed elevated levels of Angiopoietin-2, and this individual was the most inflammatory host in the cohort.
source: We then measured circulating levels of Angiopoietin-2, a biomarker of endothelium dysfunction and indicator of disease severity (Yeo et al., 2008); only one volunteer displayed elevated levels of Angiopoietin-2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b) and this individual was the most inflammatory host in the cohort (based on upregulation of plasma CXCL10 and IFNγ).
evidence: This is supported by plasma protein measurements.

claim: Only inflammatory volunteers experienced acute lymphopenia, a conserved hallmark of clinical malaria.
source: What's more, haematological analysis revealed that only inflammatory volunteers experienced acute lymphopenia, a conserved hallmark of clinical malaria (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c–d; Hviid et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by haematological data and citation.

claim: Symptomatology is not driven by the rate of parasite replication in controlled human malaria infection.
source: Symptomatology is therefore not driven by the rate of parasite replication in controlled human malaria infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between clinical score and parasite multiplication rate.

claim: Clinical outcome depends upon the intensity of inflammation, which varies widely between hosts.
source: Instead, clinical outcome seems to depend upon the intensity of inflammation, which varies widely between hosts.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong correlation between inflammation and symptoms.

claim: No metabolic signature of inflammation was robust to multiple testing when comparing inflammatory to unresponsive and suppressor hosts.
source: When we compared the three most inflammatory and symptomatic volunteers to unresponsive and suppressor hosts we could find no metabolic signature of inflammation that was robust to multiple testing (zero metabolites with an FDR-corrected p value < 0.1).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS metabolomics analysis.

claim: A conserved and persistent signature of blood-stage infection was characterized by increased adenosine, choline depletion and reduced lysoPC.
source: On the other hand, if we simply considered all volunteers as a single group and compared their post-infection time-points (day 8 and diagnosis) against pre-infection samples we could identify a conserved and persistent signature of blood-stage infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). This was characterised by increased adenosine (promotes vasodilation [Ralevic and Dunn, 2015]), choline depletion (supports parasite membrane synthesis [Witola and Ben Mamoun, 2007]) and reduced lysoPC (induces gametocytogenesis [Brancucci et al., 2017, Figure 3e–f]).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS metabolomics analysis.

claim: Volunteers who are immune quiescent are metabolically responsive to P. falciparum, and their response is indistinguishable from inflammatory hosts.
source: Evidently, volunteers who are immune quiescent are nevertheless metabolically responsive to P. falciparum, and their response is indistinguishable from inflammatory hosts.
evidence: This is inferred from the shared metabolic signature across all volunteers.

claim: Immune decision-making, systemic metabolism and parasite replication all operate independently in the early stages of the blood cycle.
source: All together, these data reveal that immune decision-making, systemic metabolism and parasite replication all operate independently in the early stages of the blood cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between these different parameters.

claim: There is a clear relationship between the intensity of inflammation and symptomatology in falciparum malaria.
source: And they further reveal a clear relationship between the intensity of inflammation and symptomatology in falciparum malaria.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis between inflammation markers and clinical scores.

claim: The inoculum used for blood challenge derived from a single malaria-infected volunteer infected by mosquito bite and was cryopreserved ex vivo after just three cycles of asexual replication.
source: In the first instance, we examined the hierarchy of var gene expression in the inoculum used for blood challenge; this derived from a single malaria-infected volunteer infected by mosquito bite and was cryopreserved ex vivo (without culture) after just three cycles of asexual replication (Cheng et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes the source and preparation of the inoculum.

claim: More than 20 var genes were highly transcribed in the inoculum.
source: In agreement, we found more than 20 var genes highly transcribed in the inoculum; notably, the expression hierarchy was dominated by group B variants and there was very low (or undetectable) transcription of most virulence-associated group A or DC8 var genes (Figure 4a and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from the inoculum.

claim: The expression hierarchy in the inoculum was dominated by group B variants.
source: In agreement, we found more than 20 var genes highly transcribed in the inoculum; notably, the expression hierarchy was dominated by group B variants and there was very low (or undetectable) transcription of most virulence-associated group A or DC8 var genes (Figure 4a and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from the inoculum.

claim: There was very low or undetectable transcription of most virulence-associated group A or DC8 var genes in the inoculum.
source: In agreement, we found more than 20 var genes highly transcribed in the inoculum; notably, the expression hierarchy was dominated by group B variants and there was very low (or undetectable) transcription of most virulence-associated group A or DC8 var genes (Figure 4a and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from the inoculum.

claim: PF3D7_0400400 encodes a group A brain endothelial cell binding PfEMP1 variant.
source: One exception was PF3D7_0400400 (previously PFD0020c), which encodes a group A brain endothelial cell binding PfEMP1 variant (Claessens et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study characterizing this variant.

claim: Group B var genes dominated the PfEMP1 landscape when parasites were isolated from the mosquito challenge cohort.
source: We further found that group B var genes dominated the PfEMP1 landscape when parasites were isolated from our mosquito challenge cohort, albeit with a higher proportion of var gene reads mapping to group A and with two DC8-like variants highly transcribed in some volunteers (PF3D7_0600200 (aka PFF0010w) and PF3D7_0800300 (aka PF08_0140)) (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from mosquito challenge volunteers.

claim: Two DC8-like variants (PF3D7_0600200 and PF3D7_0800300) were highly transcribed in some volunteers after mosquito challenge.
source: We further found that group B var genes dominated the PfEMP1 landscape when parasites were isolated from our mosquito challenge cohort, albeit with a higher proportion of var gene reads mapping to group A and with two DC8-like variants highly transcribed in some volunteers (PF3D7_0600200 (aka PFF0010w) and PF3D7_0800300 (aka PF08_0140)) (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from mosquito challenge volunteers.

claim: Malaria parasites exit the human liver expressing a diverse var gene repertoire, with variants associated with severe disease constituting a minority population.
source: Our data therefore confirmed previous observations that whilst malaria parasites exit the human liver expressing a diverse var gene repertoire, variants associated with severe disease constitute a minority population (Bachmann et al., 2019; Bachmann et al., 2016; Peters et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and citations to previous studies.

claim: After six cycles of replication in blood challenge, the expression hierarchy of var genes was essentially unchanged from that observed in the inoculum.
source: Parasites were therefore isolated from volunteers infected by blood challenge and processed immediately (without culture) for RNA-sequencing; after six cycles of replication, the expression hierarchy of var genes was essentially unchanged from that observed in the inoculum (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNA-sequencing data from inoculum and diagnosis samples.

claim: The group B var gene PF3D7_1041300 remained the most highly expressed variant in every volunteer after blood challenge.
source: Indeed, the group B var gene PF3D7_1041300 remained the most highly expressed variant in every volunteer, and transcription of group A and DC8 var genes remained low or undetectable at diagnosis (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from diagnosis samples.

claim: Transcription of group A and DC8 var genes remained low or undetectable at diagnosis after blood challenge.
source: Indeed, the group B var gene PF3D7_1041300 remained the most highly expressed variant in every volunteer, and transcription of group A and DC8 var genes remained low or undetectable at diagnosis (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from diagnosis samples.

claim: PF3D7_0400400 was functionally transcribed in the inoculum but intron-spanning reads were absent in all volunteer samples.
source: We could further highlight the significance of this result by looking only at intron-spanning reads, which must derive from functional var gene transcripts (rather than regulatory antisense transcripts, Amit-Avraham et al., 2015). We found that PF3D7_0400400 was functionally transcribed in the inoculum but intron-spanning reads were absent in all volunteer samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of intron-spanning reads in RNA-sequencing data.

claim: No var gene was more highly transcribed at the end of infection as compared to the start.
source: Differential gene expression analysis (using DESeq2) then confirmed that no var gene was more highly transcribed at the end of infection as compared to the start (adj p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: There was no preferential expansion of group A or DC8 variants within the time-frame of the blood challenge study.
source: Evidently, there was no preferential expansion of group A or DC8 variants within the time-frame of this study.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of increased transcription of these variants at diagnosis.

claim: The only rifin that was differentially expressed at diagnosis (PF3D7_0401600) was already dominantly transcribed at the start of infection.
source: When we expanded our analysis to include rifin genes we still could find no evidence of gene switching or selection. Indeed, the only rifin that was differentially expressed at diagnosis (PF3D7_0401600, log2 fold-change = 7.59, adj p=0.0002) was already dominantly transcribed at the start of infection (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis of rifin genes.

claim: There were no differentially expressed var or rifin genes between inflammatory volunteers and the rest of the cohort.
source: We therefore moved on to directly test the relationship between inflammation and parasite VSA expression. Once again, we used DESeq2 to identify differentially expressed parasite genes but this time between inflammatory volunteers and the rest of the cohort. There were no differentially expressed var or rifin genes (adj p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Only one differentially expressed parasite gene (Pfck1) could be identified between inflammatory volunteers and the rest of the cohort.
source: In fact, only one differentially expressed gene could be identified (Pfck1) - this gene encodes casein kinase one and was more highly transcribed in the inflammatory group (PF3D7_1136500, log2 fold-change = 7.32, adj p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Pfck1 encodes casein kinase one and was more highly transcribed in the inflammatory group.
source: In fact, only one differentially expressed gene could be identified (Pfck1) - this gene encodes casein kinase one and was more highly transcribed in the inflammatory group (PF3D7_1136500, log2 fold-change = 7.32, adj p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis and gene annotation.

claim: The diverse clinical outcomes observed in the blood challenge trial cannot be easily explained by variation in parasite gene expression.
source: The diverse clinical outcomes observed in this trial cannot therefore be easily explained by variation in parasite gene expression; instead, they must largely originate from host-intrinsic immune variation.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of differential parasite gene expression between groups with different clinical outcomes.

claim: The diverse clinical outcomes must largely originate from host-intrinsic immune variation.
source: The diverse clinical outcomes observed in this trial cannot therefore be easily explained by variation in parasite gene expression; instead, they must largely originate from host-intrinsic immune variation.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of differential parasite gene expression between groups with different clinical outcomes.

claim: The clinical manifestations of severe malaria depend upon host age.
source: This conclusion is well supported by epidemiological studies showing that the clinical manifestations of severe malaria depend upon host age (Dondorp et al., 2008) and children learn to tolerate high parasite densities, which could otherwise cause life-threatening disease (Gonçalves et al., 2014; Ademolue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Children learn to tolerate high parasite densities, which could otherwise cause life-threatening disease.
source: This conclusion is well supported by epidemiological studies showing that the clinical manifestations of severe malaria depend upon host age (Dondorp et al., 2008) and children learn to tolerate high parasite densities, which could otherwise cause life-threatening disease (Gonçalves et al., 2014; Ademolue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Blood-stage parasites first trigger interferon signalling in the bone marrow.
source: Recent evidence suggests that blood-stage parasites first trigger interferon signalling in the bone marrow (Spaulding et al., 2016) and the transcriptional changes we observe in whole blood are thus likely to be a signature of activated monocytes and neutrophils trafficking from bone marrow to spleen.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The transcriptional changes observed in whole blood are likely to be a signature of activated monocytes and neutrophils trafficking from bone marrow to spleen.
source: Recent evidence suggests that blood-stage parasites first trigger interferon signalling in the bone marrow (Spaulding et al., 2016) and the transcriptional changes we observe in whole blood are thus likely to be a signature of activated monocytes and neutrophils trafficking from bone marrow to spleen.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited evidence about bone marrow responses and the observed transcriptional signatures.

claim: The major secreted products of the emergency myeloid response (CXCL9 and CXCL10) specifically recruit T cells out of the circulation.
source: Furthermore, the major secreted products of this emergency myeloid response (CXCL9 and CXCL10) specifically recruit T cells out of the circulation (Groom and Luster, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge about chemokine function.

claim: The innate response to malaria quickly re-structures and co-localises key strands of the immune system.
source: The innate response to malaria therefore quickly re-structures and co-localises key strands of the immune system; whether this leads to an effective response that can limit parasite burden and minimise collateral damage will depend upon the outcome of cell-cell circuits in the spleen.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed mobilization of immune cells and chemokine production.

claim: At diagnosis, CD4+ T cells are still sequestered in the tissue.
source: Unfortunately, we cannot begin to examine these outcomes in our current datasets because at our final time-point (diagnosis) CD4+ T cells are still sequestered in the tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed lymphopenia and knowledge of T cell trafficking.

claim: Half of unresponsive volunteers (2/4) had parasite densities comparable to half of the inflammatory group (4/8) at diagnosis.
source: After all, half of unresponsive volunteers (2/4) had parasite densities comparable to half of the inflammatory group (4/8).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of parasite density data.

claim: v017 triggered a measurable inflammatory response at just 157 parasites ml−1, whereas v018 remained unresponsive at 20,000 parasites ml−1.
source: And furthermore, v017 triggered a measurable inflammatory response at just 157 parasites ml−1, whereas v018 remained unresponsive at 20,000 parasites ml−1.
evidence: This is supported by individual volunteer data on parasite density and immune response.

claim: Pushing up the pyrogenic threshold to disarm emergency myelopoiesis is a well-recognised host adaptation that promotes immune quiescence and allows individuals to transition from clinical to asymptomatic malaria.
source: Pushing up the pyrogenic threshold to disarm emergency myelopoiesis is a well-recognised host adaptation that promotes immune quiescence and allows individuals to transition from clinical to asymptomatic malaria (usually in adolescence, Gatton and Cheng, 2002; Portugal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Every volunteer increased their circulating levels of adenosine as part of a shared metabolic response to blood-stage infection.
source: Indeed, it remains a possibility that all naive hosts (including those that initially suppress genes involved in myeloid cell activation) will eventually converge on interferon-stimulated inflammation as the infection progresses. After all, every volunteer increased their circulating levels of adenosine as part of a shared metabolic response to blood-stage infection and adenosine is a potent paracrine inhibitor of inflammation (Faas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Adenosine is a potent paracrine inhibitor of inflammation.
source: After all, every volunteer increased their circulating levels of adenosine as part of a shared metabolic response to blood-stage infection and adenosine is a potent paracrine inhibitor of inflammation (Faas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: The metabolic switch to increased adenosine may represent a hardwired mechanism of self-regulation because systemic inflammation is an unavoidable fate in naive hosts.
source: This metabolic switch may therefore represent a hardwired mechanism of self-regulation because systemic inflammation is an unavoidable fate in naive hosts.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the metabolomics findings.

claim: A previous study suggested var gene expression changes within the first few days of blood-stage infection, but parasites were cultured for one month before var gene profiling.
source: This is in contrast to a previous study that suggested var gene expression changes within the first few days of blood-stage infection (Lavstsen et al., 2005). However, in that study parasites were isolated from volunteers and then placed into culture for one month before var gene profiling – switching may therefore have occurred in vitro confounding interpretation of these data.
evidence: This is supported by citation and critical evaluation of a previous study's methodology.

claim: The current study measured var gene expression ex vivo, avoiding any bias introduced by culturing parasites.
source: Our study, which measured var gene expression ex vivo, avoids any bias introduced by culturing parasites but nevertheless has limitations that require careful consideration.
evidence: This describes a methodological strength of the current study.

claim: A previous study using the same 3D7 inoculum showed var gene switching when parasites recovered from volunteers were returned to culture.
source: Nevertheless, in the absence of these data it is notable that a previous study using the same 3D7 inoculum clearly showed var gene switching when parasites recovered from volunteers were returned to culture (Peters et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In the mosquito challenge cohort there was considerable variation between volunteers in which group A and DC8 var genes were highly transcribed.
source: Furthermore, in our mosquito challenge cohort there was considerable variation between volunteers in which group A and DC8 var genes were highly transcribed, indicating that 3D7 has retained its potential to express a wide range of virulence-associated variants.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data from mosquito challenge volunteers.

claim: The incidence of severe malaria is much higher in naive hosts.
source: Nevertheless, it is clear that the incidence of severe malaria is much higher in naive hosts (Marsh and Snow, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claim: Naive hosts in endemic areas are generally infants and young children who are much less susceptible to severe disease than naive adults.
source: And moreover, naive hosts in endemic areas are generally infants and young children who are much less susceptible to severe disease than naive adults (Baird et al., 2003; Baird et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: In CHMI, volunteers recruited are those individuals who are most likely to develop life-threatening complications in the absence of drug treatment.
source: In CHMI, we are therefore recruiting those individuals who are most likely to develop life-threatening complications in the absence of drug treatment; we can therefore reasonably expect that severe disease would not have been a rare outcome of infection in our two cohorts of volunteers.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of CHMI volunteers to naturally infected populations.

claim: Parasite density is known to be an important factor in severe malaria.
source: In support of this argument, parasite density is known to be an important factor in severe malaria (Dondorp et al., 2005) and this effect could potentially be mediated by quorum sensing, which operates in trypanasomes to control their virulence (Rojas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: No external signals that can cause var gene switching have yet been identified.
source: However, no external signals that can cause var gene switching have yet been identified (Deitsch and Dzikowski, 2017; Guizetti and Scherf, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles on var gene regulation.

claim: At the mean parasite multiplication rate of 10, only 2–3 more cycles of replication would have been required for some volunteers to reach parasite burdens at which severe disease can occur (5000 parasites μl−1 or 0.1% parasitaemia).
source: However, the preferential expansion of group A/DC8 variants would need to occur rapidly because at the mean parasite multiplication rate of 10 seen in this study only 2–3 more cycles of replication would have been required for some volunteers to reach parasite burdens at which severe disease can occur (5000 parasites μl−1 or 0.1% parasitaemia [Field, 1949]).
evidence: This is calculated from the observed parasite multiplication rate and citation to historical data on severe disease thresholds.

claim: Var gene switching rates of culture-adapted parasites are low in vitro (estimated mean on-rates of 0.025–3% per generation).
source: Var gene switching rates of culture-adapted parasites are low in vitro (estimated mean on-rates of 0.025–3% per generation [Horrocks et al., 2004; Roberts et al., 1992; Ye et al., 2015]) and although mathematical modelling suggests the possibility of higher switching rates in vivo (Gatton et al., 2003) experimental data are lacking.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies measuring switching rates.

claim: Mathematical modelling suggests the possibility of higher var gene switching rates in vivo than observed in vitro.
source: Var gene switching rates of culture-adapted parasites are low in vitro (estimated mean on-rates of 0.025–3% per generation [Horrocks et al., 2004; Roberts et al., 1992; Ye et al., 2015]) and although mathematical modelling suggests the possibility of higher switching rates in vivo (Gatton et al., 2003) experimental data are lacking.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a modeling study.

claim: Rather than a sudden increase in the rate of switching, an environmental change leads to the rapid selection of variants associated with severe disease.
source: We therefore propose that rather than a sudden increase in the rate of switching an environmental change instead leads to the rapid selection of variants associated with severe disease – this could include systemic inflammation, collateral tissue damage, metabolic disturbance and/or endothelium activation.
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis based on the study findings.

claim: Group A and DC8 variants have no intrinsic growth or survival advantage; instead, their preferential expansion in naive hosts relies upon infection-induced changes in their within-host environment.
source: In this scenario, group A and DC8 variants have no intrinsic growth or survival advantage; instead, their preferential expansion in naive hosts relies upon infection-induced changes in their within-host environment.
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis based on the study findings.

claim: The responsibility for severe malaria is likely shared between parasite and host.
source: The responsibility for severe malaria is therefore likely shared between parasite and host.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed mechanism of selection requiring both parasite variants and host environmental changes.

claim: Inflammation will lead to the selection of parasites expressing group A and DC8 var genes because of cytokine-mediated upregulation of endothelial receptors such as ICAM-1.
source: In theory, inflammation will lead to the selection of parasites expressing group A and DC8 var genes because of cytokine-mediated upregulation of endothelial receptors such as ICAM-1, which is upregulated in response to TNF (Bernabeu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citation.

claim: ICAM-1 is upregulated in response to TNF.
source: In theory, inflammation will lead to the selection of parasites expressing group A and DC8 var genes because of cytokine-mediated upregulation of endothelial receptors such as ICAM-1, which is upregulated in response to TNF (Bernabeu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Enhanced cytoadherence is predicted to reduce mechanical clearance in the spleen for parasites expressing group A and DC8 var genes.
source: This is predicted to enhance their cytoadherence and reduce mechanical clearance in the spleen, as compared to parasites expressing group B and C var genes that bind only CD36 (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a prediction based on cited knowledge about cytoadherence.

claim: Parasites expressing group B and C var genes bind only CD36.
source: This is predicted to enhance their cytoadherence and reduce mechanical clearance in the spleen, as compared to parasites expressing group B and C var genes that bind only CD36 (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Circulating levels of plasma TNF had not yet increased at diagnosis in the blood challenge study.
source: However, circulating levels of plasma TNF had not yet increased at diagnosis and so more time is clearly required for interferon signalling to drive the cytokine cascades necessary to activate endothelial cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of TNF data showing elevation at diagnosis.

claim: Endothelial Protein C Receptor (EPCR) is downregulated on microvascular endothelial cells exposed to inflammatory cytokines.
source: One argument against an essential role for inflammation is that Endothelial Protein C Receptor (EPCR), currently thought to be a key receptor for cytoadherence in cerebral malaria (Turner et al., 2013), is downregulated on microvascular endothelial cells exposed to inflammatory cytokines (Bernabeu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: EPCR is currently thought to be a key receptor for cytoadherence in cerebral malaria.
source: One argument against an essential role for inflammation is that Endothelial Protein C Receptor (EPCR), currently thought to be a key receptor for cytoadherence in cerebral malaria (Turner et al., 2013), is downregulated on microvascular endothelial cells exposed to inflammatory cytokines (Bernabeu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The role of EPCR as a receptor for infected red cell binding remains controversial.
source: The role of EPCR as a receptor for infected red cell binding remains controversial (Azasi et al., 2018) but if EPCR does prove to be a major host receptor for sequestration then selection of dual-binders that also interact with ICAM-1 (Lennartz et al., 2017) would be expected in an inflammatory environment.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Pfck1 is a serine-threonine kinase that has been shown to regulate pathogen virulence in leishmaniasis and toxoplasmosis.
source: One other intriguing finding that emerged from our analysis was that parasites from inflammatory volunteers express higher levels of Pfck1 – a serine-threonine kinase (Cheong and Virshup, 2011; Jiang et al., 2018) that has been shown to regulate pathogen virulence in leishmaniasis (Dan-Goor et al., 2013) and toxoplasmosis (Wang et al., 2016), and which may be able to directly regulate type I interferon signalling (Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in other pathogens.

claim: Pfck1 may be able to directly regulate type I interferon signalling.
source: One other intriguing finding that emerged from our analysis was that parasites from inflammatory volunteers express higher levels of Pfck1 – a serine-threonine kinase (Cheong and Virshup, 2011; Jiang et al., 2018) that has been shown to regulate pathogen virulence in leishmaniasis (Dan-Goor et al., 2013) and toxoplasmosis (Wang et al., 2016), and which may be able to directly regulate type I interferon signalling (Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Immunity to severe malaria can be acquired early in life.
source: Immunity to severe malaria can be acquired early in life (Gonçalves et al., 2014) and so will require the rapid production of cross-reactive antibodies that recognise and eliminate group A and DC8 variants if these are sufficient to cause life-threatening disease.
evidence: This is supported by citation to epidemiological data.

claim: Most immune variation is underpinned by non-heritable factors.
source: An enormous body of evidence now supports the critical role of host-intrinsic variation in shaping the human immune response to pathogens and their products (Bakker et al., 2018; Brodin et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Patin et al., 2018; Piasecka et al., 2018; Ter Horst et al., 2016); remarkably most of this variation is underpinned by non-heritable factors (Bakker et al., 2018; Brodin et al., 2015; Piasecka et al., 2018; Ter Horst et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to large cohort studies.
